title: Progressives Lay the Groundwork to Force a Vote on Ending Some Arms Sales to Israel
author: Drop Site News

_Story by Tom Perkins_

Progressives in Congress are already pressuring House leadership for a vote
next session on the Block The Bombs Act, which would end U.S. sales for at
least some weapons to Israel. The organizing comes as history's most pro-
Palestinian Congress will sit in 2027, and the Congressional Progressive
Caucus (CPC) will expand its power as its membership grows to unprecedented
numbers.

Rep. Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.), who authored the current session's Block The
Bombs legislation, told Drop Site News she has already had initial discussions
with House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries about bringing the bill to the
floor, and more conversations are planned for the coming days.

Ramirez said she "did not get a direct 'no'" and she is optimistic because of
progressives' new power in Congress, Israel's dismal polling among Democrats,
and because voters sent a message by electing at least 16 new pro-peace
candidates in November, some of whom defeated among Israel's staunchest
congressional allies.

"Our caucus is going to ask the question are you pro-peace or pro-genocide?'"
Ramirez said. "The American people have made clear what side they are on, and
what they expect of their leaders."

The current Block The Bombs bill, which has 82 cosponsors, was introduced in
September 2025 and would stop the president "from selling, transferring, or
exporting certain defense articles or services to Israel, except in specified
circumstances." The sales would be allowed only if Congress passes legislation
specifying how the weapons would be used and Israel agrees to the terms. The
precise scope of next session's legislation is unclear.

In January 2026, Israel Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu [told The
Economist](https://www.economist.com/insider/the-insider/a-conversation-with-
binyamin-netanyahu) that Israel was enacting a 10-year-plan to wean itself off
U.S. weapons, and reiterated that point multiple times this year. In the days
ahead of the election, President Donald Trump said the U.S. would no longer
provide Israel with around $4 billion annually in support for weapons. On
Monday, the liberal Zionist organization [J Street called for ending taxpayer
support for sales](http://The liberal Zionist organization J Street has also
called for ending taxpayer support for sales, though stopped short of a full
embargo) and evaluating arms sales on a case-by-case basis, though it stopped
short of calling for a full embargo.

"They've become a very successful country," Trump [said on November
3](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-election/trump-says-us-will-
stop-4b-military-aid-israel-end-2026-rcna607210). "They don't need it, and we
won't be paying any more." When asked why, he added, "Why should we suffer the
slings from lunatics like an El-Sayed when they don't need it?"

Meanwhile, calls for an arms embargo that would end all weapons sales to
Israel has gained traction in the political mainstream. Among those supporting
ending taxpayer assistance and barring weapons sales are Rep. [Alexandria
Ocasio-Cortez](https://x.com/DropSiteNews/status/2077126806273163749)
(D-N.Y.), Rep. Rashida Tlaib (D-Mich.), and Senator-elect [Abdul El-
Sayed](https://abdulforsenate.com/priority/money-out-of-politics/)
(D-Mich.)--as well as incoming Reps. [Matt
Little](https://littleforcongress.com/key-issues/fighting-for-a-just-lasting-
peace-in-israel-palestine/) (D-Minn.), [Chris
Rabb](https://www.jewishvoiceforpeace.org/resource/jvp-action-
endorsements-2026) (D-Pa.), and [Melat
Kiros](https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/melat-kiros-wants-house-
votes-050310196.html) (D-Colo.).

In July this year, over 100 Democrats voted to support Republican Kentucky
Rep. Thomas Massie's
[amendment](https://legislate.dev/amendments/119/hamdt-235) to a State
Department funding bill that would have eliminated approximately $3.3 billion
in annual U.S. military assistance to Israel. The amendment still failed by a
wide margin and Massie lost his primary after Trump backed his challenger and
outside groups, including AIPAC's United Democracy Project, came in with [$37
million](https://www.lpm.org/news/2026-07-17/a-record-shattering-37m-was-
spent-on-kentuckys-massie-gallrein-race-heres-who-funded-it) in spending.

Jeffries opposed the Massie amendment and said in a letter to Democrats at the
time that it was "overly broad in that it prohibits or would limit the use of
funds for longstanding initiatives related to humanitarian aid, refugee
resettlement, peace-building and U.S. Embassy operations."

However, Jeffries also called for a "major reset" between the U.S. and Israel.

When asked about the scope of next session's Block The Bombs bill, a
spokesperson for Ramirez said the congress member did not have a comment.

A Jeffries spokesperson did not return a request for comment.

Ramirez added that she last week met with many of the pro-peace members-elect
who ran on ending U.S. support for Israel's genocide and is strategizing about
how to get the legislation to the floor. The CPC will play a key role in the
effort.

The largest CPC ever will sit next session when it takes in 25 new members,
though its total number will increase only slightly because some members are
leaving. However, this new group will be more to the left than the preceding,
and Ramirez said the caucus will be in its "strongest position ever" and is
"expanding its authority and power." Not every current CPC member cosigned on
Block The Bombs, and its leftward shift will likely increase the level of
support.

The CPC is essential to getting Block The Bombs to the floor, Ramirez said,
and she and the CPC chair, Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas), have had conversations
about it. "We are being very strategic about organizing and adding more
cosponsors," Ramirez added.

She also noted that progressives unseated staunch pro-Israel advocates like
Reps. Jimmy Gomez (D-Calif.) and Diana DeGette (D-Colo.), which gives the left
more leverage. Not only did these wins send a message to leadership, it makes
it safer for legislators who were previously on the fence to support the new
legislation.

"When you think about moving legislation you've got to ask yourself 'What are
your numbers? Where are your votes?'" Ramirez said. "And I know how to count
and the truth is we're about to have the largest CPC ever."
